tasks.title: Confirm every setting comes from configuration, with nothing environment specific left in the code.
Validate the configuration at startup and fail immediately with a clear message if it is wrong.
Make sure a failure leaves no partial work behind and reports what did not complete.
Search the whole repository and its history for anything that looks like a credential.
Run a dependency vulnerability check and read every finding.
Pin your dependency versions and record why each one is needed.
Measure how long a full run takes and how many API calls it makes.
Find one place where you are calling out more than necessary and fix it.
Record the before and after numbers in your notes.
Finalise the README with purpose, install, three usage examples, configuration and exit codes.
Include real example output for both the human and JSON formats.
Add a short section covering two design decisions and what you rejected.
Install and run the tool on a clean environment following only your own README.
Fix every instruction that failed and repeat until a clean run works first time.
Confirm the pipeline is green and every test passes.
Commit, tag a version, and pin the repository on your profile.
Run a kubectl command in JSON mode from Python and parse the result.
Print every pod with its name, status and restart count.
Notice this is the same subprocess and JSON pattern from day 146, and write that down.
Flag any pod that is not running or has restarted more than a few times.
Exit non zero when anything looks wrong so it can be used in automation.
Stop here. This is exposure, not a Kubernetes tool. Twenty minutes maximum.
List the dependencies across all three of your Python repositories.
Remove anything you are no longer using and confirm the tests still pass.
Update the pins deliberately, one at a time, checking tests after each.
Collect the patterns you look up most into one reference file.
Organise it by task: files, JSON, dates, requests, boto3, argparse, logging.
Commit it. This is the file you will actually reopen next year.
Write one paragraph describing what you can do in Python without help.
Write a second paragraph listing what you cannot do yet. Be specific.
Turn the first paragraph into one accurate line for your CV.
Open each of your three repositories as if you had never seen them and note what confuses you.
Fix the three most confusing things you found.
Order your pinned repositories so the strongest is first.
Choose one file you would be happy for an interviewer to read line by line.
Clean it: naming, docstrings, error handling and no leftover debugging.
Have the direct link ready so you can send it without hunting for it.
Write one short script. Fifteen minutes only.
Commit it.
Stop. Applications and Eid matter more than code this week.
Write or improve one small function. Fifteen minutes only.
Commit it.
Stop after fifteen minutes.
Read one file of your own code and improve one line. Fifteen minutes only.
Commit it.
Stop after fifteen minutes.
With no notes, write a script that reads a file, counts something and prints a summary.
With no notes, filter a list of dictionaries and sort the result.
Write down every single thing you had to look up.
With no notes, write a boto3 script that lists something and handles the error case.
With no notes, add argparse with one flag and structured logging.
Add these gaps to yesterday's list. This list is the point of both days.
From an empty folder, rebuild one small tool you wrote earlier, with as few lookups as possible.
Count the lookups and identify the three things you needed most often.
Drill those three until you can write them unaided.
Write the Phase 2 list: async basics, better testing, and one framework relevant to your target roles.
Set a pace for after this course that is smaller than thirty minutes but never zero.
Choose the next Python project now so there is no empty week after this ends.
Write down what you could do with Python on day 76 and what you can do today.
Write down clearly what you still cannot do, and put it next to the first paragraph.
Make sure every Python repository is committed, documented and reachable from your profile.
Decide what your fifteen minutes tomorrow will be. The plan ending is not the work ending.

questions.prompt: Why validate configuration at startup rather than when it is first used?
options: So the program fails immediately with a clear message instead of halfway through
questions.explanation: Failing at the start is the same guard clause principle you learned in bash on day 8.

questions.prompt: Why should a failure leave no partial work behind?
options: Because half finished work is harder to recover from than no work
questions.explanation: The same reasoning as trap and cleanup, applied to real operations.

questions.prompt: Why search the git history for credentials, not just the current files?
options: Because a deleted secret remains in every earlier commit
questions.explanation: Deleting a secret in a later commit does not remove it from the repository.

questions.prompt: Why run a dependency vulnerability check?
options: Because your code is only as secure as the packages it pulls in
questions.explanation: Most real world exposure comes through dependencies rather than your own code.

questions.prompt: Why record why each dependency is needed?
options: So unused packages can be removed later with confidence
questions.explanation: Nobody removes a dependency they cannot explain, so they accumulate forever.

questions.prompt: Why count the API calls a run makes?
options: Because calls cost time, money and can hit rate limits
questions.explanation: Cost and reliability both depend on how much you ask for.

questions.prompt: Why record the before and after numbers of an improvement?
options: Because a measured change is evidence and a claimed one is an opinion
questions.explanation: That number is what turns a CV line from familiar with into achieved.

questions.prompt: What should a README include beyond installation?
options: Purpose, usage examples, configuration and exit codes
questions.explanation: Someone should be able to run it correctly and interpret the result.

questions.prompt: Why show both output formats in the README?
options: Because human and machine readers need different things and both exist
questions.explanation: It also demonstrates that you thought about who consumes the output.

questions.prompt: Why install on a clean environment following only your README?
options: Because your machine has setup your instructions never mention
questions.explanation: It is the works on my machine problem, applied to documentation.

questions.prompt: Why tag a version before calling it finished?
options: So there is a specific, referenceable point someone can go back to
questions.explanation: It is the same reasoning as immutable image tags for rollback.

questions.prompt: What makes this capstone component worth showing?
options: It is tested, instrumented, documented and reproducible
questions.explanation: Those four properties are what separate software from a working script.

questions.prompt: A secret deleted in a later commit is safely removed from the repository.
questions.explanation: It remains in the history and must be treated as compromised and rotated.

questions.prompt: Validating configuration at startup makes failures easier to diagnose.
questions.explanation: The error arrives at the point where the problem is, rather than three functions later.

questions.prompt: Reducing unnecessary API calls improves both cost and reliability.
questions.explanation: Fewer calls means less spend and less exposure to rate limits and transient failures.

questions.prompt: What pattern do you use to read kubectl output from Python?
options: Run the command in JSON mode and parse the result
questions.explanation: It is the same subprocess and JSON approach you used with Terraform on day 147.

questions.prompt: What does a high restart count on a pod usually indicate?
options: The container keeps failing and being restarted
questions.explanation: It is one of the first things to look at when something is misbehaving.

questions.prompt: Why keep the Kubernetes script deliberately small?
options: Because this week is exposure, not building a Kubernetes tool
questions.explanation: Scope discipline is why the exposure week works instead of eating the month.

questions.prompt: Why does the same subprocess pattern keep appearing?
options: Because most command line tools can emit JSON, which Python reads well
questions.explanation: Learning it once gives you access to almost every tool you will meet.

questions.prompt: Why remove unused dependencies?
options: Because every dependency is maintenance and potential vulnerability
questions.explanation: Fewer packages means less to update and less to audit.

questions.prompt: Why update pinned versions one at a time?
options: So you know which update broke something when a test fails
questions.explanation: Updating everything at once turns one failure into a search problem.

questions.prompt: Why build a personal reference file of patterns?
options: Because you will look these up repeatedly and your own notes are fastest
questions.explanation: It is the file you will actually reopen, unlike a bookmarked tutorial.

questions.prompt: How should the reference be organised?
options: By task, so you find it the way you will search for it
questions.explanation: You will look for how do I read JSON, not for the letter J.

questions.prompt: Why write an honest statement of what you cannot do?
options: Because knowing your limits lets you target roles you can actually hold
questions.explanation: Getting a job you cannot do is worse than not getting it.

questions.prompt: Why turn the capability paragraph into one CV line?
options: Because a specific accurate claim beats a list of technology names
questions.explanation: Specificity is what makes a claim credible in an interview.

questions.prompt: What is the danger of overclaiming your Python level?
options: It collapses on the first practical question
questions.explanation: Interviewers ask you to write something, and the gap becomes obvious immediately.

questions.prompt: What is the danger of underclaiming?
options: You filter yourself out of roles you could actually do
questions.explanation: Calibration cuts both ways, and undervaluing yourself costs opportunities.

questions.prompt: Running a command in JSON mode and parsing it in Python works for kubectl, terraform and the AWS CLI.
questions.explanation: That single pattern covers most of the tooling you will meet.

questions.prompt: A personal reference file is a substitute for understanding.
questions.explanation: It is a shortcut for things you already understand but do not memorise, which is a different thing.

questions.prompt: An accurate self assessment is more useful in interviews than an impressive one.
questions.explanation: It is defensible, and defensible claims are what survive follow up questions.

questions.prompt: Why read your own repositories as if you had never seen them?
options: Because you cannot see what confuses a stranger while you remember writing it
questions.explanation: Familiarity hides exactly the gaps a reviewer will hit first.

questions.prompt: Why order pinned repositories with the strongest first?
options: Because a reviewer may only open one
questions.explanation: Attention is short, and the first thing they see carries the most weight.

questions.prompt: What should a code sample you send an interviewer be?
options: One file you would be happy to have read line by line
questions.explanation: One clean, complete, defensible file beats a large body of uneven work.

questions.prompt: What should you remove from a sample before sending it?
options: Leftover debugging, dead code and unclear names
questions.explanation: Those three signal carelessness more than any missing feature does.

questions.prompt: Why have the direct link ready in advance?
options: Because hunting for it during a conversation wastes the moment
questions.explanation: Small friction at the wrong moment costs opportunities.

questions.prompt: Why is this week deliberately the lightest of the whole plan?
options: Because Eid and job applications both land here
questions.explanation: Planning around known peaks is what keeps a long plan survivable.

questions.prompt: Why keep going for fifteen minutes rather than pausing entirely?
options: Because restarting a broken habit is much harder than maintaining a small one
questions.explanation: This has been the rule at every pressure point in the plan.

questions.prompt: What is the value of committing even a tiny change?
options: It keeps the daily record unbroken
questions.explanation: The record is the habit made visible.

questions.prompt: Why should applications take priority over code this week?
options: Because the applications are what actually produce interviews
questions.explanation: At this point the portfolio is built and the bottleneck is getting it seen.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of polishing code instead of applying?
options: Polishing feels productive while producing no opportunities
questions.explanation: It is a comfortable substitute for the uncomfortable task, which is the trap.

questions.prompt: How many strong repositories do you actually need?
questions.explanation: Three lets you show range without any of them being weak.

questions.prompt: What should improving one line a day teach you?
options: That small consistent effort compounds and keeps the habit alive
questions.explanation: It is the sustainable pace this whole track has been training.

questions.prompt: Polishing your portfolio further is a reasonable substitute for sending applications.
questions.explanation: It feels productive and produces nothing, which is exactly why it is tempting.

questions.prompt: A reviewer may open only one of your repositories.
questions.explanation: Which is why order and consistency across all three matter.

questions.prompt: Fifteen minutes on a heavy week is enough to protect a daily habit.
questions.explanation: Continuity matters far more than volume at the pressure points.

questions.prompt: Why do a retention audit with no notes?
options: Because completing something and retaining it are different
questions.explanation: Interviews and incidents happen without your notes.

questions.prompt: What is the point of the list of things you looked up?
options: It tells you exactly what to drill next
questions.explanation: The list is the output of the exercise, and acting on it is the value.

questions.prompt: Why rebuild a tool from an empty folder?
options: Because it measures what you can produce unaided
questions.explanation: Counting the lookups gives you an honest measure of fluency.

questions.prompt: What is a realistic description of your Python after nine months of half hour days?
options: Able to write, test, package and instrument small tools
questions.explanation: That is a genuinely useful level, and it is what you can defend.

questions.prompt: Why choose the next project before this plan ends?
options: So there is no empty week where the habit dies
questions.explanation: The gap after a finish line is where momentum is usually lost.

questions.prompt: What is a sustainable pace after an intensive plan?
options: Smaller than before, but never zero
questions.explanation: Skills decay, and a small daily floor preserves far more than occasional bursts.

questions.prompt: Why write down what you still cannot do?
options: Because it makes your claims about what you can do credible
questions.explanation: Calibrated self assessment is rare enough that it stands out.

questions.prompt: What single pattern from this track transfers to almost any tool?
options: Run a command in JSON mode and parse the output
questions.explanation: It worked for the AWS CLI, Terraform and kubectl without changing shape.

questions.prompt: What did building your own API client before boto3 achieve?
options: It made boto3 understandable rather than magical
questions.explanation: Understanding the shape of a thing before meeting the library is a repeatable strategy.

questions.prompt: Why did this track stay at thirty minutes a day?
options: So it never damaged the main track it was supporting
questions.explanation: Two tracks only work when the smaller one genuinely stays smaller.

questions.prompt: What is the most valuable thing you built in this track?
options: A tool that reads real infrastructure, handles failure, and is tested and documented
questions.explanation: It solves a real problem end to end, which is what portfolio evidence means.

questions.prompt: What does finishing this plan actually mean?
options: One stage is done and the next begins tomorrow
questions.explanation: The plan ending and the work ending are not the same thing.

questions.prompt: Being able to write something with your notes open is the same as being able to write it in an interview.
questions.explanation: The gap between the two is exactly what these last days are designed to measure.

questions.prompt: Deciding tomorrow's fifteen minutes before the plan ends protects the habit you built.
questions.explanation: The undefined day after a finish line is where most people quietly stop.

questions.prompt: Thirty minutes a day for nine months is enough to become a competent scripter for infrastructure work.
questions.explanation: It is not enough to become a software engineer, and it is exactly what these roles ask for.
